# Test Case Validation API

Status: a Test Case submission is schema-checked, then checked against the Term
and Symbol Rules bound to each Field, each Rule suppressed where its own
Exceptions permit. A Test Case producing any Violation is rejected and left
unwritten; one producing none is written through to TestLink over `testlink-mcp`.
Reading a stored Test Case serves it whole, with whatever the Rules found in it
attached beside it. Test Cases, Test Suites and Projects can each be created,
read, updated and deleted. Reference documents are served read-only from the
database, checked the same way a test case is. Rule sets live in that database
too, written there by an operator with SQL and read once at startup. Every
response names the version of the rule set that produced it, and each violation
is logged so a repeatedly firing rule is visible.

## What this is

An API server that sits in front of `testlink-mcp`. AI agents submit test cases
to it; it checks each field against a rule set; cases that pass are written
through to TestLink, cases that fail are rejected with reasons the agent can act
on. Agents also read existing cases and reference documents through this API.

It exists because the agent that generates test cases cannot reliably check its
own output, so checking is moved somewhere the agent cannot reach or modify.

## Running it

The database is not optional — the rule sets and the reference documents live in
it, and the server reads it at startup. TestLink is optional for the test suite,
which runs against a stubbed one, and needed for the checks that suite cannot
make: that a write lands, and that the id it answers with is the id a read
answers to.

```
cp .env.example .env
docker compose up -d          # the database, and TestLink at http://localhost:8090
psql postgres://validator:validator@localhost:5433/validator -f schema.sql
```

The connection string is spelled out rather than read from `.env`, which is a
file the server loads and not one your shell has exported. It is the address the
compose file publishes on; if you changed `DATABASE_URL`, use what you changed it
to. Give the database a moment to come up before the third line, or `psql` will
answer that nothing is listening yet.

`psql` is a client you install separately, and a host running Postgres in Docker
often does not have one. Where it is missing, the container brought up above
carries its own, and everything below works the same through it:

```
docker compose exec -T validator-db psql -U validator -d validator < schema.sql
```

There is a starting point you can apply instead of writing rules from nothing.
`default-rules.sql` holds the checks for the thing this project exists to catch —
a test case that reads as though a model wrote it — 74 terms and 15 symbols drawn
from six published anti-AI-writing references rather than invented here. Applying
it is optional, and it is applied the way the schema is:

```
psql postgres://validator:validator@localhost:5433/validator -f default-rules.sql
```

```
docker compose exec -T validator-db psql -U validator -d validator < default-rules.sql
```

Each of those 89 checks is written against all five fields, enabled, so 445 rules
arrive. Applying the file again changes nothing, so a rule you have since
switched off stays off.

It is meant to be tuned down rather than accepted whole. `ensure that` and
`correctly` are ordinary QA English, and applying it will reject test cases a
tester wrote by hand. Switch off what earns nothing, the way
[Changing what is there](#changing-what-is-there) describes.

Now write your rules and reference documents. Nothing in this project writes to
the database (ADR-0006) — you do, with SQL, using whatever client you already
have. The two statements below are the whole of it, and the suite extracts and
runs them, so what is written here is what a Postgres accepts and what the server
reads back.

Your rules. A rule is a row (ADR-0007): it names the field it binds to, the kind
of check it is, what it looks for and the reason a caller is given. Add one, or
switch one off, with a statement naming that rule alone.

```sql
insert into rules (rule_id, content_kind, field, category, looks_for, reason) values
  ('no-verify-that', 'testCase', 'name', 'term', 'verify that',
   'Name what the test checks, not that it verifies.'),
  ('no-utilise', 'testCase', 'summary', 'term', 'utilise',
   'The product documentation says use, not utilise.'),
  ('no-utilise', 'referenceDocument', 'body', 'term', 'utilise',
   'The product documentation says use, not utilise.');
```

A reference document. The id is what a caller retrieves it by; the title and the
body are the two fields the rules reach:

```sql
insert into reference_documents (id, title, body) values (
  'roaming',
  'Roaming between access points',
  'A client moves between access points without dropping its session.'
);
```

An apostrophe inside either is written doubled, the way SQL takes it.

Then start the server:

```
npm run dev
```

It refuses to start until an enabled rule is there, because a server with nothing
to check with would accept everything.

### What a rule may carry

The example above shows term rules only. Every shape, for reference:

```sql
-- A term matches a word or phrase, as written but in any casing.
insert into rules (rule_id, content_kind, field, category, looks_for, reason) values
  ('no-utilise', 'testCase', 'preconditions', 'term', 'utilise',
   'The product documentation says use, not utilise.');

-- A symbol matches a single character. `whitespace` is the one value `flanked`
-- takes, and narrows the rule to where whitespace is on both sides, which leaves
-- the character inside a word alone. Leave it null to fire wherever the
-- character is.
insert into rules (rule_id, content_kind, field, category, looks_for, flanked, reason) values
  ('no-standalone-dash', 'testCase', 'preconditions', 'symbol', '-', 'whitespace',
   'A dash between words is punctuation; standing alone it is a bullet.');

-- An exception permits the narrow case it names, and nothing else. It suppresses
-- only the rule it belongs to, and belongs to exactly one.
insert into rules (rule_id, content_kind, field, category, looks_for, reason) values
  ('no-ap', 'testCase', 'preconditions', 'term', 'AP', 'Write access point in full.');

insert into rule_exceptions (rule, phrase)
  select id, 'AP isolation' from rules
  where content_kind = 'testCase' and field = 'preconditions' and rule_id = 'no-ap';
```

A rule names `testCase` or `referenceDocument` as its content kind, and a field
that kind has — `name`, `summary` and `preconditions` for a test case, `title`
and `body` for a reference document. Naming anything else is refused by the
schema as you write it, rather than binding to nothing and silently never firing.

Rule ids are unique per field, not overall, which is why the exception above is
found by all three columns. The same id on two fields is two rules, and both are
worth having.

### Changing what is there

Ordinary SQL, and when it takes effect differs by kind. A document is read per
request, so an `update reference_documents ... where id = ...` is live on the
next one, and a `delete` stops it being served. Rules are read once at startup
and never reloaded, so nothing you write to `rules` reaches anything until you
restart the server.

Switch a rule off rather than deleting it:

```
update rules set enabled = false
where content_kind = 'testCase' and field = 'summary' and rule_id = 'no-utilise';
```

It stops firing just as completely, and the row stays so a violation already
logged against it can still be explained. For the same reason, do not edit what a
rule looks for — a changed check under an unchanged name makes every violation
already logged describe something that never happened. Add a new rule and switch
the old one off. The reason is editable; it is what the caller is told, not what
is looked for.

Neither is enforced by the schema, by decision rather than oversight — ADR-0007
records why, and what to add on the day that stops being true.

The TestLink image is the `testlink-code` fork rather than upstream TestLink,
because updating a project needs `tl.updateTestProject`, which upstream does not
ship. Nothing outside this repository has to be cloned or kept in step.

The compose project is now named `testcase-validator` rather than
`testcase-validator-testlink`, because it brings up more than TestLink. Docker
names volumes after the project, so **anyone who ran the old compose file gets a
fresh, empty TestLink** — including a new API key to generate. The old volumes
are still there under `testcase-validator-testlink_*` if anything in them was
worth keeping.

One step is not automated: **the API key**. TestLink generates it under _My
Settings → API interface_, with the XML-RPC API enabled for the installation.
A server brought up fresh has no key until someone makes one, so this is not
yet one command from nothing to a verifiable environment. See issue #13.

## Read first

- `CONTEXT.md` — the vocabulary of this project. Use these words exactly.
- `schema.sql` — the tables you apply, and what each column is for.
- `default-rules.sql` — default rules for AI writing tells, to apply and tune down.
- `docs/adr/0001` — validation sits outside the agent's trust boundary
- `docs/adr/0002` — detection is deterministic; no model in the request path
- `docs/adr/0003` — the generating agent works only over the API, never local files
- `docs/adr/0004` — rule sets live in a database, read once at startup
- `docs/adr/0005` — reference documents are checked content, held in that database
- `docs/adr/0006` — rule sets and documents are written with SQL; no loader ships
- `docs/adr/0007` — a rule is a row, and is disabled rather than deleted
- `docs/adr/0008` — a default set of rules ships as SQL the operator applies

## Decided

- Validation is per field, each field with its own rule set.
- Rules match terms (words, in any casing) and symbols (characters) literally.
  No inference.
- An Exception is a word or phrase attached to a single Rule, permitting the
  narrow case it names and nothing else. Any Rule can carry them; no Rule shares
  them.
- Rule sets are supplied by the user at deployment. Configuring them is a user
  task, not something the framework decides.
- A failed validation rejects the write. There is no partial or provisional
  write, and no validate-only endpoint.
- Responses are stateless. A rejection lists every violation, each with field,
  rule id, reason, matched text and character offset. No suggested replacement.
- The read path serves stored content unchanged, with any violations attached as
  metadata, so agents do not copy patterns the write path would reject. No
  violation refuses a read, however many fire, because refusing would put the
  content out of reach.
- Violations on a read are found at read time against the rules running now, so
  a read reports what submitting that content would report.
- A read answers with the content under `testCase` and the violations beside it,
  never merged into the served fields.
- A read of an id TestLink holds nothing under answers with a client error;
  a read attempted while TestLink is unreachable answers with a server error. The
  two are told apart by status code alone, so a caller retries the one and
  escalates the other. Neither carries violations, so neither reads as a
  rejection. The TestLink client reports absence as an answer rather than as a
  failure, so the read path never infers it from an error message.
- Every response names the rule set version, so a violation traces to the rules
  that were in force rather than to whichever rules are running when it is read
  back. The version is derived from the rules in force rather than declared by an
  operator alongside them: a hand-typed version goes on naming rules that have
  since been changed, which is the confusion a version is kept to prevent. It
  covers what a caller was judged by and nothing else — the field, the rule id,
  the kind of check, what is looked for, the flanking, the reason and the
  exceptions — so a rule switched off and later switched back on returns the
  version to what it was rather than to a new one meaning the same thing.
- The version rides on a `Rule-Set-Version` header, which reaches every response
  including a delete that has no body at all, and in the body as
  `ruleSetVersion` wherever the rules judged what was sent, because callers are
  agents that read the body. A schema refusal and a response TestLink held
  nothing for carry the header but no field: no rule took part in either, so
  neither claims a version in what it says.
- Violations are logged one line per violation on the write paths, carrying the
  rule id, the field and the rule set version. A rule firing over and over is
  what separates a rule that cannot be satisfied from an agent that writes badly
  once, and that shows as repeated lines for one rule id. Nothing is counted in
  the server and nothing is read back, so the server stays stateless and no
  logged data reaches a validation outcome: content is judged the same way
  however often it is submitted, and a rejection repeats word for word. What a
  successful write answers with is not identical, because the id is TestLink's
  to assign. Reads do not log — what a read finds is a rule firing on content
  already stored, not an agent submitting the same mistake again.
- TestLink is reached through `testlink-mcp`, which the server spawns and speaks
  to over stdio. testlink-mcp answers every call in text, so the one place that
  reads absence out of that text is the TestLink client — narrowly, from what
  TestLink reported about the call and never from the content it served, because
  a test case is entitled to be about a file that does not exist. Anything the
  client cannot place is escalated as an outage, so no unrecognised failure is
  ever answered as "not there".
- The client expects testlink-mcp **1.6.0**, and launches that version rather
  than `latest`. A tag is not a version: Docker will not re-pull one it already
  holds, so a host that pulled `latest` before a tool existed keeps a server
  without it. A server missing a tool the client calls says so and names the
  version expected, rather than reading as TestLink being unreachable — the
  fault is the version, and TestLink is reachable and healthy.
- Which project and which suite a submission is placed in are the caller's to
  say, per submission: TestLink is the store the agent works in, not a fixed
  drawer. The author login the validator writes as is deployment config.
- Creation and update are told apart by status code, so a caller knows whether
  it added a test case or replaced one without reading the body. An update is a
  write, so the rules run on it exactly as they run on a submission. An update
  that omits an optional field leaves TestLink's existing value alone rather
  than clearing it — testlink-mcp ignores an empty field, so emptying one is not
  reachable through this API.
- Fields are written through to TestLink exactly as submitted, and served back
  exactly as stored. testlink-mcp documents summary and preconditions as HTML,
  but wrapping on the way in would mean serving markup a caller never wrote, and
  the read path is contracted to serve stored content unchanged. The consequence
  is real and unresolved: where a case was authored in TestLink's own editor, the
  stored field holds markup, so violations found on a read carry offsets that
  point into tags. Worth its own ticket.
- Projects and test suites are served straight through, unchecked: no rule binds
  to either. Both can be created, listed, updated and deleted.
- Reference documents are served over the API so the generating agent has no
  local files at all, which is what ADR-0003 asks for. A caller lists them and
  retrieves one by id; no path reaches the API, so there is no filesystem for a
  caller to describe or to walk out of. An id nothing is held under answers a
  client error carrying no violations, so it cannot be read as a rejection, and
  is told apart from the database being unreachable by status code alone.
- A reference document is checked content, not a file served through. It has a
  title and a body, each with its own rule set, and a read carries whatever
  fired. ADR-0003's reasoning is the whole point: the read path is where legacy
  fingerprints propagate into new cases, and a document written in the wording
  the rules exist to catch is the most direct way for that to happen. A read is
  never refused, however much fired, for the same reason a test case read is not.
- Reference documents are read-only over the API. A document the agent could
  write is one it could author in the style the rules catch and then read back as
  authority — the same reason it cannot reload a rule.
- The fields of a test case and of a reference document never overlap, and
  neither do their rule sets. A rule set is written under the content it checks,
  `testCase:` or `referenceDocument:`, so loosening a rule on one cannot quietly
  loosen the other. A rule set naming anything else stops the server starting.
- Rule sets and reference documents live in a database (ADR-0004, ADR-0005),
  written by an operator with SQL and read by the server (ADR-0006). The project
  ships no write path at all: the object the server holds exposes no write, and
  neither does anything else here, so relaxing a rule or authoring a document is
  not something the running system can do. Rule sets are appended rather than
  replaced, so superseding one does not destroy the one a running server is still
  judging by; nothing in the API resolves a version back to its row, so that is
  history kept cheaply rather than a lookup offered.
- A reference document's shape is what an operator writes: the id a caller
  retrieves it by, and its two fields. The title is kept out of the body so a
  rule firing in it is reported once rather than under both fields. Nothing
  validates a document before the server serves it — its fields are whatever was
  written.
- The schema ships as `schema.sql` for an operator to apply, because the server
  only reads and so is never the thing that creates what it reads from.
- A database the schema has never been applied to is told apart from one that is
  unreachable. The server asks whether the tables are there rather than reading
  that out of the error a missing table raises, so a fresh database is answered
  with what to do rather than with a stack trace.
- Deleting a project cascades to every suite, case, plan, build, execution and
  requirement under it, so the caller restates the project's own prefix as
  `?confirmPrefix=`. Restating it wrongly deletes nothing and answers a conflict
  — told apart from the project not being there and from TestLink not answering,
  because all three would otherwise reach the caller as the same failure.
- Updating a project needs a TestLink providing `tl.updateTestProject`, which
  ships in the `testlink-code` fork rather than upstream. A server without it is
  the operator's to fix, so it answers as a server error rather than as a
  project that is not there.
- Ollama runs offline to survey the corpus and surface candidate rules a human
  then writes. It is never in the request path.
- Node.js 18 or later, TypeScript, ESM. Fastify for HTTP, chosen because field
  structure is already constrained by a schema and Fastify validates request
  bodies against JSON Schema natively — so malformed submissions are refused
  before any rule runs, and the two produce different response shapes.
- A rule is a row in the database, added and switched off one at a time, and read
  from it once at startup and never reloaded. There is no reload endpoint, so the generating
  agent has no mechanism by which it could relax a rule that keeps rejecting it.
  This also closes the tension the README used to flag against ADR-0001, which
  says rules are "baked into the deployed image rather than read from a mounted
  path": there is no mounted path any more. What ADR-0001 protects is unchanged.
- No rule applies across all fields, and there is no inheritance between fields.
- The server holds no state between requests. What the database holds is the
  operator's configuration and the operator's reference material, both read-only
  from the server's side, so the same test case submitted twice is still answered
  identically.
- Vitest, exercising four seams: the HTTP surface with a stubbed TestLink client
  and a stubbed document store, application startup with the rules a database
  answered with, the real TestLink client over a stubbed tool caller, and the real
  store over both a stubbed query seam and an in-process Postgres. The last two
  exist because the first is deliberately stubbed — the suite must not need a live
  TestLink or a live database — which would otherwise leave the tool calls, the
  SQL, and the reading of what comes back untested. No test reaches into the
  matcher or the offset calculator directly.

## Not decided

- Deployment shape.
- Whether the database becomes the source of truth imported into production
  TestLink, or a cache in front of it. ADR-0004 left this open and ADR-0005 did
  not close it.

## Out of scope

Duplication detection, ambiguity detection, requirement traceability, and a
generation harness for test plans and test cases. Each is a separate project.

81	fire inside a longer word, where a word runs on through a hyphen or an
82	underscore. The words of a phrase are matched however they are spaced, a line
83	break included.

88	matched as a word, a Symbol as a character.

90

93	character, so the same character stays legal inside a word without needing an
94	Exception. The edge of a field counts as whitespace, so a character opening or
95	closing a field is flanked. Distinct from Exception: Flanking narrows where a
96	rule looks, an Exception suppresses it where it would otherwise fire.

98	
99	**Exception**:
100	A word or phrase attached to a rule that suppresses it where the rule's match
101	falls inside it, leaving the rest of the field under the rule. Written the way a
102	Term is and found the same way — in any casing, however its words are spaced —
103	but found wherever it turns up, inside a longer word included.
104	An Exception belongs to exactly one rule — there is no shared exception list.
105	_Avoid_: allowlist, whitelist, ignore list, false positive, override
106	
107	### Outcomes
108	
109	**Violation**:
110	One rule firing on one field, carrying the reason returned to the caller. The
111	unit of everything the API reports; a response is a list of violations.
112	_Avoid_: error, issue, finding, warning, failure, defect
113	
114	**Rejection**:
115	The API's refusal to write a test case through to TestLink because it produced
116	at least one violation. Rejection is the only failure mode — there is no partial
117	or provisional write.
118	_Avoid_: block, reject state, quarantine, fail

_Avoid_: check, constraint, assertion, validator

**Rule Set**:
The rules bound to a single field. Every field has its own; there is no global
rule set applying across fields. Not a thing written down anywhere — each rule
names the field and the content it belongs to, and a rule set is the enabled ones
that name a given field. So a rule is added or switched off on its own, and no
rule can reach a field it was not written for.
_Avoid_: profile, policy, ruleset, config

**Rule Set Version**:
What names the rules a response was produced by, carried on every response. Derived
from the rules in force rather than declared beside them, so it cannot go on naming
rules that have since been changed. It covers everything a caller was judged by —
the field, the rule id, the kind of check, what is looked for, the flanking, the
reason and the exceptions — and leaves out disabled rules, which judge nothing. The
id is in there though nothing looks for it in a field, because it is what a
violation carries: two rule sets a caller reads differently are not one. The same rules
always produce the same version, so a rule switched off and later switched back on
returns the version to what it was rather than to a new one meaning the same thing.
Fixed for the life of a running server, because rules are read once at startup and
never reloaded.
_Avoid_: revision, build, tag, release, hash

**Term**:
A word or phrase a rule looks for in a field — either vocabulary that must be
used or wording that must not appear. Matched whole and in any casing: a term is
written once rather than once per capitalisation it turns up in, and it does not
fire inside a longer word, where a word runs on through a hyphen or an
underscore. The words of a phrase are matched however they are spaced, a line
break included.
_Avoid_: keyword, word, phrase, vocabulary, jargon

**Symbol**:
A single character a rule looks for in a field. Distinct from Term: a Term is
matched as a word, a Symbol as a character.
_Avoid_: special character, punctuation, glyph, sign

**Flanking**:
A condition on a symbol rule that fires it only where whitespace surrounds the
character, so the same character stays legal inside a word without needing an
Exception. The edge of a field counts as whitespace, so a character opening or
closing a field is flanked. Distinct from Exception: Flanking narrows where a
rule looks, an Exception suppresses it where it would otherwise fire.
_Avoid_: word boundary, padding, delimiter, spaced

**Exception**:
A word or phrase attached to a rule that suppresses it where the rule's match
falls inside it, leaving the rest of the field under the rule. Written the way a
Term is and found the same way — in any casing, however its words are spaced —
but found wherever it turns up, inside a longer word included.
An Exception belongs to exactly one rule — there is no shared exception list.
_Avoid_: allowlist, whitelist, ignore list, false positive, override

### Outcomes

**Violation**:
One rule firing on one field, carrying the reason returned to the caller. The
unit of everything the API reports; a response is a list of violations.
_Avoid_: error, issue, finding, warning, failure, defect

**Rejection**:
The API's refusal to write a test case through to TestLink because it produced
at least one violation. Rejection is the only failure mode — there is no partial
or provisional write.
_Avoid_: block, reject state, quarantine, fail

# Detection is deterministic; the model never decides a violation

Every violation is produced by literal term or symbol matching, not by a language
model. A local model is used offline to survey the corpus and surface candidate
rules a human then writes; once written, that rule is deterministic forever and
the model has no further part in it.

## Considered Options

Running fields through a local model in the request path was the obvious reading
of "validation with Ollama" and was rejected. The API sits in a write path and
returns rejections an agent must act on, which requires verdicts that are

A 9B model gives neither.

The model's role shrinks over time rather than growing — each rule promoted from
survey to rule set is one less thing needing inference. Detection classes that
cannot be expressed as literal matching (duplication, ambiguity, unstated
preconditions) are out of scope until a deterministic expression is found.

# `analysis-sut` — /home/jack/src/testcase-validator

Derived from code first (steps 1–4), docs read last and only to contradict (step 5).

---

## #1 — A validate-then-write gate in front of TestLink, with no write path back to its own configuration

**Key point.** Every write route runs the Rules *before* it calls TestLink and returns 422 without writing; every read route runs the same Rules and never refuses; and the object holding the Rules and Reference Documents exposes no write at all, so the running system cannot relax a Rule or author the material it validates against.

**Ground truth.**
`/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/violation.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/reference-document.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/postgres-store.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/testlink-client.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/server.ts`

**Mechanism.** `buildApp({ testlink, documents, rules, logger })` takes three collaborators and defines 16 routes. On `POST /projects/:projectId/suites/:suiteId/test-cases` and `PUT /test-cases/:id`, the handler's first statement is `findViolations(request.body, bound.testCase)`; if `violations.length > 0` it `return reject(...)` — 422, `{ violations, ruleSetVersion }` — and `testlink.createTestCase` / `testlink.updateTestCase` is never reached, so a rejected Test Case is unwritten by construction rather than by rollback. `GET /test-cases/:id` and `GET /reference-documents/:id` call the same `findViolations` (against `bound.testCase` and `bound.referenceDocument`) and always answer 200 with the content and the violations as sibling keys — `versioned({ testCase, violations })` — never merged into the served Fields, never refused (`app.ts:236-240`, `app.ts:422-430`). `DELETE /test-cases/:id` and all eight `/projects` and `/suites` routes run no Rule at all; `app.ts:276-278` says why: no Rule binds to a Project or Test Suite. On the config side, `DocumentStore` declares exactly `listDocuments()` and `getDocument(id)`, `PostgresStore` implements those plus `rules()`, and there is no insert/update/delete anywhere in `src/` — the only writer of `rules`, `rule_exceptions` and `reference_documents` is an operator running `psql`.

**Why it matters.** A newcomer looking for the "validation service" finds no validate-only endpoint and no rule-management API, and could conclude validation is advisory. It is not: the gate is the write path itself, and the asymmetry (writes refused, reads never refused) is the whole design — a read that refused would put the offending content out of reach of the agent that has to fix it.

**Diagram.**
```
  generating agent  ── HTTP only, no files, no DB, no TestLink ──┐
                                                                 v
 +--------------------------- buildApp (app.ts) -----------------------------+
 | POST /projects/:p/suites/:s/test-cases      PUT /test-cases/:id           |
 |   1. testCaseSchema (Fastify ajv, coerceTypes:false)                      |
 |   2. findViolations(body, bound.testCase)                                 |
 |        any -> reject() 422 { violations, ruleSetVersion }                 |
 |               testlink.* IS NEVER CALLED                                  |
 |   3. testlink.createTestCase / updateTestCase                             |
 |                                                                           |
 | GET /test-cases/:id            GET /reference-documents/:id               |
 |   findViolations(...) -> 200 { testCase|document, violations, version }   |
 |   never refused, however many fired                                       |
 |                                                                           |
 | DELETE /test-cases/:id | /projects * | /suites *   -> no Rule runs        |
 +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+
        | read+write                              | read only
        v                                         v
  McpTestLinkClient -> testlink-mcp -> TestLink   PostgresStore
                                                  rules() listDocuments()
                                                  getDocument()  <- no write
                                                  method exists in src/
```

**Contradicts.** none.

---

## #2 — What a Rule actually does to text: word-standing Terms, single-character Symbols, and Exceptions that suppress by span containment

**Key point.** A Term fires only where the match stands as a word (a word runs through `-` and `_`), in any casing, with the phrase's internal spacing relaxed to `\s+`; a Symbol fires on every occurrence of one character unless `flanked='whitespace'` narrows it, where the edge of the Field counts as whitespace; an Exception suppresses a match only when the match falls wholly inside a span the Exception matched, and only for the Rule it belongs to.

**Ground truth.**
`/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/violation.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/rule-set.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/schema.sql`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/default-rules.sql`

**Mechanism.** `findViolations(content, ruleSets)` iterates the `Map<field, RuleSet>` it was handed, skips any Field whose value is `undefined`, and dispatches per Rule to `termViolations` or `symbolViolations`. `matcherFor(term)` escapes regex metacharacters, rewrites `\s+` to `\s+`, and compiles with flags `giu` — so `wireless network` matches across a line break. `standsAsWord` then rejects a hit whose neighbour character matches `/[\p{L}\p{N}_-]/u`, which is why `no-utilise` leaves `utilises` and `re-utilise` alone. `symbolViolations` walks `value.indexOf(symbol, …)` and, when `rule.flanked === 'whitespace'`, requires `isGap` on both sides, where `isGap(undefined) === true`. Suppression is `suppressedSpans(value, rule.exceptions)` — the Exception is matched by the same `matcherFor` but with **no** word-standing test, so it matches inside longer words — and `isSuppressed` requires `offset >= span.start && offset + text.length <= span.end`. Each Violation carries `{ field, rule, reason, text, offset }` with `text` being the casing found, not the casing written, and no suggested replacement. `schema.sql`'s `a_symbol_is_one_character` check uses `looks_for like '_'` (one character, not one byte) and `rule-set.ts`'s `checkStoredRule` re-checks it as `[...looksFor].length !== 1`; the shipped `default-rules.sql` writes 74 Terms and 15 Symbols against all five Fields = 445 rows (verified by counting the file).

**Why it matters.** This is the entire definition of "violation" in the product — everything else is plumbing. A newcomer who assumes substring matching will mispredict every result, and an operator writing rules cannot reason about `default-rules.sql`'s 445 rows without knowing that `-` inside a word is a word character to a Term and a whitespace-flanked target to a Symbol.

**Diagram.**
```
findViolations(content, ruleSets)                          violation.ts
  for [field, rules] of ruleSets:
      value = content[field]        undefined -> Field skipped entirely

   TERM                                  SYMBOL
   spansOf(value, rule.term)             indexOf(symbol) loop
     matcherFor: escape metachars          flanked === 'whitespace' ?
     \s+ -> "\s+" ; flags 'giu'              isGap(before) && isGap(after)
   standsAsWord(start, text)                 isGap = /\s/ OR edge of Field
     isOutsideAWord = NOT [\p{L}\p{N}_-]   else fires on every occurrence
     'utilise' misses 'utilises'
     and 're-utilise'
          \                                   /
           fired[] --------------------------+
                                             |
   suppressedSpans(value, rule.exceptions)   |   <- this Rule's phrases only
     same matcherFor, NO word-standing test  |      (no shared list exists)
                                             v
        isSuppressed: offset >= span.start
                   && offset + text.length <= span.end
                                             v
        Violation { field, rule, reason, text, offset }   (no replacement)
```

**Contradicts.** none. (`CONTEXT.md`'s Term, Symbol, Flanking and Exception entries match the code line for line, including "the edge of a field counts as whitespace".)

---

## #3 — Five answer shapes, decided by pattern-matching testlink-mcp's prose, and anything unrecognised escalates as an outage

**Key point.** A caller tells apart schema refusal (400), Rejection (422), nothing-there (404), wrong prefix (409) and outage (500) by shape alone, never by reading a message — and the classification is made in one place, `McpTestLinkClient.place()`, by three narrow regexes with `throw` as the default.

**Ground truth.**
`/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/mcp-testlink-client.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/tool-caller.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/stdio-tool-caller.ts`

**Mechanism.** `app.setErrorHandler` turns any `error.validation` into `400 { refusal:'schema', message }` — carrying no `violations`, so it cannot be misread as a Rejection, and no `ruleSetVersion`, because no Rule ran. `reject()` produces `422 { violations, ruleSetVersion }`. `nothingThere()` produces `404 { message: 'TestLink holds no …' }` — no `refusal`, no violations, no version. `answer(tool, args, alsoTheCallers?)` makes exactly one tool call and reads the result three ways: `result.isError`, or `reportedProblem(content)` (TestLink puts a `code` + `message` where a result should go), then `deniedIn(content)` (`status === false` → throw). `place()` checks, in order: `reportsUnconfirmed` = `/Confirmation failed/i` → `unconfirmed` → route answers `409`; `reportsMissingTool` = `/Unknown tool/i` → throw naming `expectedTestLinkMcp = '1.6.0'`; `reportsAbsence` = `/does not exist|not found/i` → `absent` → route answers 404; **everything else throws**, so an unrecognised failure is an outage, never a "not there". Absence is read only out of what TestLink said *about the call*, never out of served content (`mcp-testlink-client.ts:205-221`). `idOf()` throws when a create answered with no id at top level or in `additionalInfo`, and treats `0` and `''` as no id — a write that "succeeded" without an id is a failure. `listProjects` and `createProject` also throw on `absent`, because nothing was named to be missing.

**Why it matters.** The whole boundary is text over stdio (`ToolResult` is `{ text, isError }` and nothing more). A newcomer will look for structured error codes and find two regexes; without knowing the default is `throw`, they cannot see that adding a fourth wording is the standing maintenance cost, nor why 404 and 500 are the two halves of the same failure.

**Diagram.**
```
 caller             app.ts                       McpTestLinkClient.answer()
   |
   |-- bad body ---> setErrorHandler (error.validation)
   |                 400 { refusal:'schema', message }      no Rule ran
   |
   |-- violations -> reject()
   |                 422 { violations, ruleSetVersion }
   |
   '-- clean ------> testlink.<op> ----> tools.call(tool, args)  [stdio text]
                                              |
                     isError  OR  reportedProblem(first().code+message)
                                              v  place(tool, message)
             /Confirmation failed/i  -> unconfirmed ---> 409 conflict
             /Unknown tool/i         -> throw  "older than 1.6.0" -> 500
             /does not exist|not found/i -> absent -> nothingThere() 404
             anything else           -> throw  "could not be reached" -> 500
                                              |
                     deniedIn: first().status === false      -> throw -> 500
                     idOf: no id / '' / 0 on a create        -> throw -> 500
```

**Contradicts.** none.

---

## #4 — Startup is the only moment Rules enter the process, it refuses in three distinct ways, and the version it derives is stamped on every answer but claimed only by answers the Rules judged

**Key point.** `src/server.ts` reads the Rules once and dies rather than start degraded — missing setting, zero enabled rows (including a database with no schema at all), or a row that cannot be bound — and the `sha256`-derived `Rule-Set-Version` is then fixed for the process, sent as a header on every reply including a 204, but present in a body only where a Rule contributed to it.

**Ground truth.**
`/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/server.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/setting.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/rule-set.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/postgres-store.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/src/app.ts`, `/home/jack/src/testcase-validator/package.json`

**Mechanism.** `required(name)` throws `"<NAME> is not set, so this will not run."` for `DATABASE_URL`, `TESTLINK_URL`, `TESTLINK_API_KEY`, `TESTLINK_AUTHOR_LOGIN` (`PORT` is *not* required — `Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000)`). `store.rules()` first asks `select 1 from information_schema.tables where table_name = 'rules'` and returns `[]` when the schema was never applied — a fresh database is "no Rules", not an outage — then reads `where enabled order by id` and attaches enabled `rule_exceptions` gathered in a second statement rather than a join. `server.ts:22-26` throws on `rules.length === 0` with the message telling the operator to apply `schema.sql`. Then `bindRules` → `checkRules` collects **every** problem before `refuse()` throws one multi-line report, so an operator fixes them together. `ruleSetVersionOf(rules)` hashes the sorted, canonical JSON of `[contentKind, field, ruleId, category, looksFor, flanked, reason, sortedExceptions]` — excluding the row id and the row order — and slices 12 hex chars, so disabling and re-enabling a Rule returns the version to its old value. `app.addHook('onSend')` sets `Rule-Set-Version` on every reply; `versioned(body)` adds `ruleSetVersion` to 422s, successful writes and reads, and is deliberately *not* applied to the 400 or the 404. `reject()` also emits `request.log.warn({ ruleSetVersion, field, rule }, 'Rule violated')` once per violation, on write paths only, with nothing counted or read back. Nothing under `test/` imports `src/server.ts` — `package.json` reaches it only through `"dev": "tsx --env-file-if-exists=.env src/server.ts"`.

**Why it matters.** It explains why the API has no reload and why an operator's `update rules …` appears to do nothing: the process is judging by a snapshot. It also explains the one thing a caller can rely on across time — the version — and the deliberate rule that a 400 or 404 names no version, since no Rule took part.

**Diagram.**
```
 npm run dev -> tsx src/server.ts        (no file under test/ imports this)
   required('DATABASE_URL' | 'TESTLINK_URL' | 'TESTLINK_API_KEY'
            | 'TESTLINK_AUTHOR_LOGIN')  -- unset --> throw, no server
   connectToPostgres -> PostgresStore(queriesFrom(pg.Client))
   store.rules()
        hasSchema? select 1 from information_schema.tables ... 'rules'
             no -> []            (fresh DB = "no Rules", NOT an outage)
        select ... from rules where enabled order by id
        + exceptionsByRule: rule_exceptions where enabled order by id
   rules.length === 0 -----> throw "Apply schema.sql and insert a Rule"
        |
        v buildApp({ rules })
   bindRules -> checkRules  collects EVERY problem -> refuse() one report
   ruleSetVersionOf = sha256( sorted JSON of
       [contentKind, field, ruleId, category, looksFor, flanked,
        reason, exceptions.sort()] ).slice(0,12)   <- fixed for process
        |
        +-- onSend hook: Rule-Set-Version header on EVERY reply (204 too)
        +-- versioned(): ruleSetVersion IN BODY only where Rules judged
              422, 201/200 writes, reads   |   NOT on 400 schema, NOT 404
```

**Contradicts.** `docs/adr/0001-…md:5-6` — "Rules are baked into the deployed image rather than read from a mounted path". Half of this is false in the code: Rules are rows read from Postgres at startup and the image contains none. (`README.md:351` and `docs/adr/0004-…md:26-27` both flag the drift; ADR-0001 itself carries no note.) The other half — no reload endpoint — is true: no route mutates `bound` or `ruleSetVersion`.

---

Two behaviours are, at the four-point cap, explained only inside another point's mechanism, and I name them rather than let the count hide them:
